Enslavement is the act or process of forcing a person — or a group of people — into slavery: a condition where they are completely stripped of their freedom, their rights over their own body and life, and are controlled by another person or group who treats them not as human beings but as property.

A simple way to think about it: if freedom is the right to live life on your own terms, enslavement is the violent, deliberate removal of that right.
Two ways the word is used: as a process, and as a state

The word "enslavement" can describe two things, which are closely related but slightly different.

First, it can describe the act or process of forcing someone into slavery — the capturing, coercing, buying, or trapping of a person to bring them into that condition. In this sense, you might say: "The enslavement of indigenous peoples was a defining horror of colonialism." Here, the word is pointing at the action — someone actively doing this to someone else.

Second, it can describe the condition or state of being enslaved — the ongoing reality of living under slavery. For example: "Many were born into enslavement and knew nothing else." Here, the word is pointing at the lived situation — what it means to exist inside that condition.

Both uses are correct and common, and context usually makes clear which one is meant.

In its most serious and direct meaning, enslavement refers to what has happened throughout human history — and still happens in certain forms today — when people are stripped of their freedom and forced to serve others as property. The most widely known example is the transatlantic slave trade, during which millions of Africans were captured and subjected to enslavement across the Americas and the Caribbean over several centuries. But enslavement has existed in many forms across many different civilizations and time periods.

In this literal sense, enslavement typically means: being forced to work without pay and without any ability to leave; having no legal rights over your own body, your family, or your choices; being bought and sold like an object; being denied access to education, movement, and basic human dignity. The word carries enormous moral weight because it represents one of the most extreme violations of a person's humanity.

Beyond the literal, "enslavement" is also widely used in a metaphorical sense — to describe any situation where a person is so completely dominated or controlled by something that they feel powerless to escape it, even if no physical chains are involved.

For example, you might hear: "His enslavement to money drove every decision he made" — meaning he was so consumed by the pursuit of money that it controlled him entirely. Or: "The enslavement to debt" — meaning a person so buried in what they owe that they feel they have no freedom left. Other common figurative uses include enslavement to addiction, to fear, to a habit, or even to technology.

In these cases, the word is chosen deliberately because it captures something stronger than just being "influenced" or "distracted." It describes a feeling of being trapped and helpless — where the controlling force (money, addiction, debt, etc.) acts like a master and the person has lost the ability to simply walk away.

These two words are very close, and you will often see them used almost interchangeably. However, there is a subtle but real difference in their emphasis.

Slavery tends to refer to the institution, the system, or the general condition — the broad phenomenon as it exists. "Slavery existed for centuries across the ancient world."

Enslavement, on the other hand, tends to emphasize the act of forcing someone into that state — the doing of it, the imposition of it by one person or group upon another. "The enslavement of millions was a deliberate crime against humanity."

Think of it this way: slavery describes the house; enslavement describes the act of dragging someone inside and locking the door.
The word family — related forms you will encounter

Since you will often see these related words in the same context, here is how they connect:

To enslave is the verb — the action. "They enslaved the population after conquering the region."

Enslaved is the adjective — it describes someone in that condition. You will often hear the phrase "enslaved people" or "enslaved persons," which is widely preferred today over the older word "slave" because it keeps the focus on their humanity — they were people first, and enslavement was something done to them.

An enslaver is the noun for the person who does the enslaving — the one who imposes the condition.

Slavery is the broader noun for the system or institution itself.

A slave is the traditional noun for a person subjected to slavery, though as mentioned, "enslaved person" is increasingly preferred in careful, respectful writing.
A final thought to anchor the meaning

The power of the word "enslavement" — what makes it different from words like "control" or "restriction" — is its implication of total loss. It is not partial. It is not temporary inconvenience. Enslavement, whether literal or figurative, means that a person's will, autonomy, and self-determination have been taken away so completely that they exist to serve something or someone other than themselves. That totality is what the word always carries with it, in every context you encounter it.
